sections.h2: Who buys in Arlington and how fast can they close?
sections.html:
Three kinds of buyers show up in Arlington: families with a mortgage, individuals paying cash, and investors who will take a house whatever its shape. How fast you close is up to them. Cash can fund as soon as title work wraps up, but a loan has to clear an appraisal and underwriting first.

An estimated 402,134 people lived in Arlington in mid-2025. Owners occupy 54.3 percent of homes, a little over half, so your house competes with many rentals and other resales.

  • Financed buyer: tends to pay top price for an updated house, though a low appraisal or a bad inspection can end the deal.
  • Individual cash buyer: will still ask for repairs and usually wants a normal inspection period.
  • Investor: prices in the repairs, skips showings, and will pick a date that fits your move, a probate schedule or a lender's deadline.

In the newest five-year estimates, the middle Arlington owner-occupied home is worth $304,700 and the middle rent is $1,470 a month. A worn house, or one in a less popular pocket, will land under those numbers.

About 86.7 percent of residents over age one lived at the same address a year earlier, a sign of settled neighborhoods. Houses from the postwar boom stand next to newer subdivisions, so look over the roof, foundation and wiring of an older house before a buyer's inspector does.

The permit for a short-term rental stays with you. Arlington issues each one to a single owner for a single address, with no transfer or assignment allowed, so the next owner has to file a new application.

Arlington counts any home, or part of one, rented for fewer than 30 consecutive days as a short-term rental. Eligible areas include a zone built around the Entertainment District, medium-density and multifamily residential districts, and some commercial and mixed-use districts. Rentals already operating when the rules started were not grandfathered.

  • Guests are capped at two per bedroom plus two more, never above 12.
  • No amplified sound or outdoor gatherings between 10 p.m. and 9 a.m.
  • Turning other space into bedrooms is banned and can reduce the headcount allowed.
  • Three citations within a year, or ten days of ignoring a written notice, can end in revocation.

If your house hosted guests, gather the permit and the inspection checklist results before you show it. The city's short-term rental page lists what inspectors check, including smoke alarms, escape windows, a posted floor plan and a fire extinguisher.

Values are set as of January 1, and whoever owns the house that day is responsible for the year's tax. Bills reach Arlington owners around October 1, and homestead value notices arrive near April 1. To dispute a value, file a protest with the appraisal review board by May 15 or 30 days after the notice, whichever comes later.

Most accounts are due January 31. Splitting the bill in two is allowed, with halves due November 30 and June 30. After the January deadline, February 1 adds a six percent penalty and one percent interest, and the penalty reaches 12 percent by July. Since the lien attaches in January, even a March closing must clear that year's bill.

  • The school district exemption on a homestead is $140,000.
  • Owners who are 65 or older, or disabled, receive a further $60,000 school exemption plus a school tax ceiling.
  • A buyer who moves in after a post-January 1 sale may qualify for the exemption immediately if you never claimed it.

The state posts its full calendar on the Comptroller's deadlines page. To get a payoff for your own account, call the Tarrant County offices that serve your address.

Title changes hands when a signed and acknowledged deed enters the property records of the county that holds the lot. Texas will not file a conveyance until a notary or similar officer has taken the signer's acknowledgment, or two witnesses have sworn to it.

Pull these together before you take an offer:

  • your current deed and photo ID
  • mortgage and home-equity payoff statements
  • this year's tax statement and any back-tax notices
  • HOA payoff and transfer paperwork, if one applies
  • leases, deposits and tenant contacts, if someone lives there
  • any rental permit and inspection records

Inherited houses need the correct title document. An executor signs an executor's deed. When a will goes through probate with no administration, a muniment of title order does the job. An affidavit of heirship carries less weight: it is just a sworn statement, unverified by any court, and a title company can turn it down.

After you sign, the title company requests a tax statement and each payoff letter, then searches for liens and open city notices. Bring photo ID and your current deed to the signing. A buyer will also ask for the lease and deposit details if someone lives in the house.

Arrange a walk-through date with the buyer and decide who keeps keys, garage openers and appliance manuals. Small agreements like these, written into the contract, prevent last-minute friction on the day the house changes hands. Cancel your own utilities and insurance only after funding is confirmed, not before.

Money changes hands once both sides have signed, and the deed then goes to the county clerk. Hold on to your settlement statement. It lists every payoff taken from your proceeds, useful if a lender or the tax office asks for proof later.

Work out what each route puts in your pocket once payoffs, repairs and waiting time are counted. Listing can bring a higher price for a well-kept house. Selling for cash gets rid of the repair list, the open houses and the danger of a buyer's loan collapsing.

Insist that offers be written out with the price, closing date, settlement charges and any exit clauses. Find out if the buyer will take the house with a tenant in it or with city notices still open. Take away your payoffs and carrying costs, then pick the number and date that suit you.

For a vacant house or one needing big repairs, ask each buyer who handles utilities, insurance and access until closing. Buyers differ more on these points than on headline price, and a written answer protects you if the closing slips.

faqs.q: Will a buyer pay for a house in Arlington that needs a new roof?
faqs.a: Yes. Investors and cash buyers routinely accept roof work and lower the offer to match. You repair nothing before closing, so weigh the bid against a repaired house's price minus your own repair bills.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in Arlington that has been used as an Airbnb?
faqs.a: Yes. The permit does not convey, so the buyer applies fresh and must pass the city's inspection. Tell buyers plainly whether the address sits inside an eligible zone.

faqs.q: What happens to unpaid tax when my Arlington sale closes?
faqs.a: The amount owed is taken from your proceeds when you sign, because the lien remains on the house. Request a payoff figure from the tax office early to avoid a surprise on the closing statement.

faqs.q: Where is the deed filed after an Arlington sale?
faqs.a: The county clerk for the county that holds the house, which is Tarrant County for most Arlington addresses. If your lot is near a county line, check the tax bill.
About 402,134 residents in 2025, with 142,455 households and 95.87 square miles of land.
